🇲🇽🚆 <u>Valley of Mexico Gets Its First New Metropolitan Plan Since 1998</u>

Mexico City, the State of Mexico, Hidalgo and Morelos, together with the federal urban development ministry Sedatu, are updating the Valley of Mexico metropolitan zoning program for the first time since 1998. The plan covers transport, water supply, drainage and protected green areas across 84 municipalities and boroughs, a region of about 22.7 million people. Public consultation is open until November 22.
banner: VALLEY OF MEXICO: FIRST PLAN SINCE 1998

🚨🇲🇽 <u>US Treasury Blacklists 21 People and 25 Firms Tied to 'Mayito Flaco'</u>

OFAC sanctioned 21 people and 25 companies linked to Los Mayos, the Sinaloa Cartel faction led by Ismael Zambada Sicairos. The list includes Carlos Torres Torres, ex-husband of Baja California governor Marina del Pilar, whom Washington accuses of using political influence to shield the cartel, and former Mexicali police chief Pedro Ariel Mendivil. Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit ran its own review, found "risky financial operations and irregularities" among some of those named, and added them to Mexico's blocked-persons list, noting this does not establish guilt. The faction's founder, El Mayo Zambada, was taken illegally from Mexican territory in July 2024, and that abduction has still not been explained.
banner: OFAC: 46 TARGETS TIED TO MAYITO FLACO

🇲🇽🏥 <u>12,000 New Hospital Beds by 2030, Double What 36 Neoliberal Years Built</u>

Public health will gain 12,000 new hospital beds by 2030: 4,800 from hospitals built in 2019-2024 and 7,400 planned for 2024-2030, with more than 180 billion pesos invested. Over 36 years of neoliberal governments, Mexico built about 6,000. "It was a very great abandonment that put tremendous pressure on health institutions," Sheinbaum said. Deputy health minister Eduardo Clark reported 33 hospitals opened in the first two years, with 1,535 new beds, and 45 more hospital projects under way.

🇲🇽📚 <u>Young Women Drive Drop in Mexico's Share of Youth Neither Studying Nor Working</u>

The OECD's Education at a Glance 2026 shows that the share of Mexicans aged 18-24 who neither study nor work fell from 23% in 2015 to 19% in 2025. Most of the drop came from young women getting into classrooms and jobs. Over the same decade, the share of 25-34-year-olds without upper-secondary schooling fell from 55% to 40%. Mexico is still above the OECD average of 13%, and 3 in 10 young women remain out of both, mostly because of unpaid care work.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>UN Refugee Chief: Mexico Shows Asylum and Security Can Coexist</u>

At a solemn session of the Mexican Senate, UNHCR head Barham Salih said Mexico "has built a strong legal framework for the protection of refugees" and, while asylum systems elsewhere are under pressure, "continues to demonstrate that protection can be maintained in practice." He also announced an agreement with the government to advance México Integra, a plan to make refugee integration national policy across federal and local government, business and universities. The same day, the US Supreme Court cleared deportations to third countries.
banner: UNHCR: MEXICO SETS THE ASYLUM EXAMPLE

🇲🇽📉 <u>The Fed Raises Rates, and the Peso Closes Above 18</u>

The peso closed at 18.06 per dollar, down 0.66% on the day. It is the first close above 18 since March 30, El Economista reports. The drop began after the Federal Reserve's 25-basis-point hike on September 16, which ate into the carry trade. A global risk-off mood, driven by the Middle East and rising oil prices, did the rest. Banxico held its rate at 6.5% and chose not to react mechanically.
banner: PESO: FIRST CLOSE ABOVE 18 SINCE MARCH

🇲🇽🏭 <u>New IMSS Hospitals Approved for Irapuato and Celaya</u>

IMSS chief Zoé Robledo confirmed to CTM leader Tereso Medina that hospital projects for Irapuato and Celaya have been approved. Workers in Guanajuato's industrial corridor had pushed for them because the rise in formal jobs outgrew the hospital beds. The Celaya hospital will serve the whole Laja-Bajío region. Growth that fills the IMSS rolls has to fill hospital wards too.
banner: IMSS: TWO NEW HOSPITALS FOR THE BAJÍO

🇲🇽🚆 <u>Almost 9 Billion More Pesos to Rebuild Flooded Northern Veracruz</u>

The federal government added nearly 9 billion pesos to its 2026 budget to rebuild roads and bridges wrecked by the October 2025 floods in northern Veracruz. The SICT will repair 36 roads and 18 bridges across 14 municipalities. Road work is 40% done, and the target is to finish in the first quarter of 2027. Governor Rocío Nahle admits some bridges are still pending; three go back out to tender after the first bid drew no one.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Economy Ministry Revokes 189 Export-Maquila Permits</u>

The Economy Ministry cancelled 189 IMMEX programs held by companies that never filed their 2025 sales and export report. Those firms lose the right to import inputs duty-free. The ministry suspended them on June 30 and gave them until the end of August to comply. The list names mining, auto-parts and apparel firms, among them Compañía Minera Cuzcatlán and BPI Braking Systems. Tax-free imports come with paperwork attached.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>US Parking-Meter Firm Sued Mexico for 600 Million Pesos. It Lost, and Now It Pays</u>

ICSID threw out the whole NAFTA claim that Doups Holdings brought against Mexico over Mexico City parking-meter concessions. The tribunal ruled it had no jurisdiction: Doups had agreed to be treated as Mexican for its investment, never proved it controlled Pagomet, and skipped NAFTA's required steps. Four years of litigation ended with Doups ordered to pay Mexico more than $1 million in costs.
banner: ICSID: MEXICO BEATS US FIRM, 600M PESOS
